Trump dismisses concerns over the rapid pace of AI research, following days of warnings from experts in the field about possible existential risks.
In a meeting with US officials, the Houthis promise not to attack American or any other commercial vessels, with the exception of those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
September 14
The yield on benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury notes rises above 5% for the first time since October 2023, amid a global bond sell-off as surging oil prices and disruption to Middle Eastern energy supplies fuel renewed fears of inflation. The yield reaches 5.01%, while Brent crude rises above $108 a barrel.
U.S. Senator Mitch McConnell returns to the Senate floor following a three-month absence.
Trump announces that he is willing to engage with Iran to negotiate a deal.
Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding celebration is reported to have been partly funded by a Russian oligarch with close connections to President Vladimir Putin.
A court in Boston blocks Trump restrictions on how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the country.
The Supreme Court rejects the Trump administration's request to lift an injunction blocking new United States Postal Service restrictions on mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections.
The US Space Force announces that the country now has weapons deployed in orbit, suggesting that the unspecified platforms are needed to compete with adversaries China and Russia.
September 15
The US military announces that it destroyed two Iranian small boats the day before following an IRGC attempt to capture one of its Navy drones patrolling the Strait of Hormuz.
A federal judge blocks the Kennedy Center from adding President Trump's name to the building or its grounds without congressional approval. Hours later, the centre's board votes to close most of the venue for up to two years for renovations.
September 16
Three people are killed in a helicopter crash in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, including NBC News journalists Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw.
The Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time in three years, from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.
A memorandum of understanding is signed with the Pakistan army by US drone maker Powerus, which is set to merge with a firm backed by Trump's sons.
The Trump administration announces that Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation are barred from attending the UN General Assembly in New York, accusing them of breaching US law.
September 17
The House of Representatives passes sweeping Russia sanctions legislation by a vote of 262–159.
Flash flooding in the Navajo Nation kills three.
A UN mission finds grounds to believe that the US committed war crimes in the 2026 Minab school attack and the 2026 Lamerd sports hall attack.
Lockheed Martin receives the first batch of Patriot interceptor parts from General Motors less than a month after the two companies signed a manufacturing agreement, in a success for the Pentagon's push for faster weapon production, particularly the Patriot missile defense system, as it remained one of the world's most sought-after weapons for the US war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine.
The US sanctions Iranian financier Babak Zanjani's cryptocurrency exchange for enabling the Iranian government and processing payments for ships to safely transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US announces that it will restrict "luxury splurge" shopping by the Iranian government during the UN General Assembly.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation approves a debt facility worth up to $414 million for Canadian miner Global Atomic's Dasa project in Niger, which the company describes as the highest-grade uranium deposit in Africa.
September 18
Russia and China veto a US proposal for UN experts to continue monitoring UN sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program.
The US sentences a Syrian national who fraudulently immigrated to the country and served as the former head of the notorious Adra Prison under former Syrian president Bashar al-Assad to 60 years imprisonment on torture charges.
Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news."
Greenland crisis: The United States, Denmark and Greenland announce an agreement to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, expanding the permanent U.S. military presence in Greenland while recognising Danish sovereignty and Greenlandic self-determination. The agreement follows months of threats by President Trump to acquire or annex Greenland.
September 19
The Trump administration approves a potential $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine, adding that the country would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US foreign military financing.
Trump signs the "Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," which allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on Russian oil buyers, including China and India, in response to the country's war in Ukraine, as well as to extend existing sanctions on Iran.
The United States Southern Command states that its strike on a vessel in the Caribbean killed four people, adding that confirmed intelligence indicated the vessel's active participation in narco-trafficking.
Sanctions against Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki's People's Front for Democracy and Justice and Eritrean forces are lifted by the Trump administration "to advance US regional interests" in the Red Sea.
September 22 – The cybercrime group ShinyHunters claims to have breached the Federal Bureau of Investigation's jobs portal and stolen personal data belonging to thousands of current and former FBI employees and job applicants. The FBI opens an investigation, while Reuters partially verifies a sample containing names, addresses, Social Security numbers and details of sensitive intelligence assignments.
September 23
Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian arrives in New York to speak at the United Nations General Assembly, the first time an elected leader from a nation at war with the United States sets foot on American soil to address a UN gathering.
Movie magnate Harvey Weinstein is sentenced to 15 years in prison after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.
September 24
A federal judge rules that Trump's White House ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico likely breached the First Amendment and due process clause and orders access to be reinstated.
The Navy confirms that eight sailors from the USS Lincoln group, which spent a record-setting amount of time at sea in support of the Iran war, attempted suicide.
Iraqi authorities announce that the US transferred the diplomatic and logistics hub at Baghdad International Airport to Iraq prior to the withdrawal of American soldiers from the country.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping meets Trump at the White House during his first visit to Washington in a decade. The two leaders discuss trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and international conflicts, and agree to extend the existing US–China trade truce by two months.
September 25 – Cities and states across the U.S., including Lexington, Nashville, New Orleans, and Portland, hold commemorations honoring former American country singer Dolly Parton including the 9 to 5 song one month after her death. California becomes the first U.S. state to designate September 25 as Dolly Parton Day.
September 26
A powerful nor'easter strikes the northeast United States. A New York City Housing Authority employee is killed by a falling tree in Brooklyn.
Trump rejects Iran's seven-day ceasefire proposal over nuclear concerns.
September 28
SpaceX's Starship achieves orbit for the first time, and deploys 26 "next generation" Starlink V3 satellites.
OpenAI announces that it will cancel the release of GPT-6.1, the next version of ChatGPT amid ongoing safety concerns. The company also issues an update on recent incidents during which its AI model hacked into other websites.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio orders that the Iranian delegation to the UN General Assembly immediately leave the country after overstaying amid stalled negotiations to end the war between both nations.
September 29
The US sanctions ten people and entities in various jurisdictions that have acquired weapons and their parts for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics.
The X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain closes permanently following a series of lawsuits alleging brain injuries.
September 30
The Trump administration concludes the withdrawal of US soldiers from their final bases in Iraq, marking the end of the US-led coalition's war against ISIL.
A US defense contract for counter-drone systems is awarded to the Israeli company SMARTSHOOTER.
Syria is removed from the US munitions export prohibition list.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirms that the American military will reduce 20% of its generals and admirals.
The Office of Religious Affairs is established.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit temporarily halts the execution of Christa Gail Pike, but the U.S. Supreme Court later allows it to proceed. Pike survives two doses of pentobarbital and is hospitalized, prompting Tennessee governor Bill Lee to suspend the state's remaining 2026 execution and order an independent review.
An immigration judge rules that Trump can deport the Palestinian-born leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque—an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights—who does not have a criminal record in the US, where he has lived since 1993 on national security grounds, citing his imprisonment in Israel in 1988 after being convicted of throwing stones at Israeli military personnel in the West Bank.
The United States Senate confirms Keith Sonderling as the 31st United States secretary of labor by a 47–41 vote.


=== October ===
October 1
The US imposes new sanctions on Iran, targeting rail, automotive, manufacturing, and steel sectors, as well as overseas suppliers, saying that the goal is to economically isolate the Iranian government.
The U.S. military starts sending about 9,000 soldiers to the Middle East on naval ships, such as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group and the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group.
October 2
The US imposes sanctions on Hamas' financing network, which includes two French-based funds.
Alabama state representative Brett Easterbrook is arrested on charges of first-degree human trafficking and prostitution as part of a sting. At least a dozen other men are arrested.
October 3 – Trump establishes a task force to examine the risks and opportunities of AI and recommend what role the federal government should play in overseeing the technology without compromising competitiveness with China.
October 4
Two people are killed while 35 others are injured in a block party shooting in Vienna, Georgia.
The State Department announces the expulsion of two members of the Iranian delegation who attended the recent United Nations General Assembly after they ignored an order to leave the country long after the General Assembly had ended.
Trump withdraws all U.S. bombers from RAF Fairford, a British air base targeted by an attack that the UK linked to the Iranian government, due to urgent concerns about a potentially complex drone attack ordered by the IRGC as part of a plot to target the aircraft and kill American soldiers at RAF Fairford, which is loosely modeled after Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb.
The FBI arrests Chinese American Wanying Zhang at Los Angeles International Airport for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent of China and surveilling the family of President of Taiwan Lai Ching-te in the United States.
October 5
The Trump administration authorizes a $1 billion munitions sale to the UAE for up to 10,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon Systems, as well as a $400 million sale of "repair and return services" for Patriot missiles to Kuwait.
Trump states that he remains "always open" to direct negotiations with Tehran.
The US announces that foreign financial institutions doing business with Iran may be sanctioned without warning.
October 6
Paramount Skydance completes its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, in one of the largest media mergers in history. The deal combines two of Hollywood's largest film studios with major television and streaming businesses including CBS, CNN, HBO and Paramount+, with the combined company renamed Skydance Corporation.
Trump authorizes execution by firing squad for the Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan.
The US destroys an Iranian-connected boat conducting surveillance after its crew was safely evacuated.
October 7
The US and Greece agree on a coordinated security framework for counterterrorism information sharing among respective law enforcement agencies.
The Wall Street Journal reports that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle asked Republican donor Eric Deters to pay off $100,000 in credit card debt in exchange for access to the Trump administration, six days before her July 2025 Senate confirmation hearing. Guilfoyle's attorney said that any payments from Deters were for appearances.
October 8
The US begins direct negotiations with the military junta of Myanmar while continuing sanctions against its leader, Min Aung Hlaing, for human rights violations, notably the Rohingya genocide.
The US imposes additional sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet.
Trump instructs the Pentagon to prepare military options in case active combat operations against Iran resume even as he said on that day that strikes would not renew prior to the midterm elections on November 3.
October 9
The US sanctions the International Criminal Court, stating that it will never allow the court to prosecute American soldiers. The sanctions occurred after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to former ICC judge Navi Pillay, and Trump criticized the decision on Truth Social.
During a White House event, Trump declares that the war with Iran will "be over soon, one way or the other," suggesting that the almost eight-month-old conflict would either be resolved diplomatically or militarily.
Trump announces that he secured Russian president Vladimir Putin's agreement to release diesel into U.S. and worldwide markets.
Trump names Katie Zacharia as the new White House Press Secretary, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.
Nine people are killed in a gun attack in Erie, Pennsylvania.
October 10
Hundreds of thousands of Americans in Alabama and the Florida panhandle are without electricity after Hurricane Isaias hits the U.S. Gulf Coast. Trump cancels his intentions to attend a football match between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa, citing a desire not to impede emergency response operations, and declares a state of emergency in Alabama and Florida.
The American military announces that it disabled a cargo ship attempting to violate its naval blockade of Iran.
The Justice Department announces that it is probing whether major television networks breached federal antitrust laws by collectively refusing to cover the White House.
October 12
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Department of Homeland Security agents search the home of representative Ilhan Omar in Washington, D.C., as part of an "ongoing investigation".
October 13
October 2026 white powder incident: An unmarked white powder is mailed, alongside threats, to dozens of state election officials and members of Congress, sparking fears of anthrax. The powders are later shown to be salt or yeast.
Following a request from Trump, Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns. Her resignation comes following multiple reports on her conduct, including one alleging that Guilfoyle asked a Republican donor to pay off her credit card.
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis is sentenced to 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.
Trump says the US will make a decision on Iran "very soon", describing it as a "failed country" and claiming its inflation has reached 300%. His remarks coincide with reports that Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged renewed military action against Iran before the 27 October Israeli election, which Netanyahu's office denies.
October 14 – Israel agrees to purchase 12 Boeing Apache helicopters.
October 15
Authorities investigate letters containing "suspicious substances" mailed to congressional and election offices, suggestive of a similar threat in 2023.
The US issues new sanctions against Iran, targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities.
A mass shooting occurs outside an elementary school in Oregon killing four people, including three children.
October 16 – Katie Zacharia is fired after just five days as White House Press Secretary.
October 18 – Ukrainian president Zelenskyy says that the United States has started sharing intelligence again with Ukraine.
October 19
Trump introduces the $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program, which will deliver one-time emergency financial aid to U.S. farmers struggling with record-high production expenses during the peak of the harvest season.
The Supreme Court rejects a bid to restore a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the suspected 9/11 mastermind.
Trump authorizes the creation of a National Institutes of Health division and a new White House task force to "advance the cause of women's health".
October 20 – Trump signs an act into law designating the Chiricahua National Monument near Willcox, Arizona, as a national park, the first new national park in six years.
October 21
Russian president Vladimir Putin announces the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher who had been imprisoned by Moscow on charges of serving as a foreign combatant for Ukraine.
The U.S. sanctions a Panama- and Greece-based law firm, stating that it facilitated Iran's shadow fleet for years and indirectly supported the Iranian government's capacity to produce income to fund its nuclear program.
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin reach a 10-year agreement to manufacture 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets.
The pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC announces it will stop endorsing political candidates and making direct PAC contributions.
October 22 – The Department of Justice accuses the Democrats of promoting a spoiler candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent candidate Dan Sullivan in the 2026 United States Senate election in Alaska to confuse voters. The DOJ sues the state of Alaska to block the results if Senator Sullivan loses the election by a small margin.
October 23
The White House announces that a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been agreed by President Putin and President Zelenskyy, mediated by First Lady Melania Trump.
President Trump confirms that Starlink service has been restored for Ukraine.
October 27 – A grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson over her January 6 testimony.
October 28
In an attempt to resume peace talks, Vice President JD Vance sends a letter to Iranian National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei at Trump's directive.
The District Court for the Eastern District of New York convicts a US woman of receiving Islamic State training after marrying an Islamic State militant at the age of 18.
The Milwaukee Brewers defeat the Tampa Bay Rays to win the 2026 World Series, their first championship in franchise history.
October 29
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fires Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the U.S. military's chief military planner.
QatarEnergy announces a long-term liquefied natural gas procurement agreement with the United States until 2054.
October 30
TRM Labs, an American blockchain analysis firm, reveals that North Korea's Bureau 121 was responsible for a $6.3 billion theft on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, the largest heist in history, prompting an investigation by the FBI and the US Secret Service.
The Trump administration authorizes the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine.


=== November ===
November 1
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut is hospitalised after suffering a stroke.
A Learjet 60 crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board.
Democratic Representative Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers over Democratic Abdul Al-Sayed in the Senate election in Michigan. Al-Sayed had previously defeated Stevens in the primaries. In response, Stevens's staff resign and the Michigan Democratic Party revoke Stevens's party membership.
November 2
Small-scale, "defensive" strikes are carried out by the US against Iranian positions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington state resident dies of bird flu.

November 3
2026 United States midterm elections: In a blue wave, the Democratic Party wins majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Trump announces that the US will terminate all military aid to Israel, totaling $4 billion per year, by the end of 2026, but will continue to sell military hardware.
November 4
First Lady Melania Trump receives the Order of Princess Olga from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for her significant personal contribution to humanitarian relief efforts in Ukraine.
The US imposes new sanctions on companies and individuals in India and Turkey with ties to the Iranian government.
